notes.key_messages:
• Questions where candidates had to deduce the molecular formula of a compound were well answered.
• Questions involving balancing equations were well answered. Some candidates struggled to calculate
the relative molecular mass of a given compound in Question 4(c).
• Questions on the more detailed aspects of the kinetic particle model were not answered well. There was
a tendency for candidates to get arrangement, separation and motion mixed up.
• It is important that candidates read the question carefully to understand what exactly is being asked.
Practice of reading and interpreting questions that involve data handling should also be prioritised.
• Candidates struggled to answer chemical test questions correctly. Their answers showed many large
gaps in knowledge. This is a part of the syllabus that needs to be practiced and used in classroom tests
more often. Candidates struggled with ‘Describe a test for iodide ions’ in Question 2(b).
• Organic Chemistry questions were not answered well. Candidates struggled to draw the displayed
formula of ethanoic acid in Question 3(b)(i) and many struggled to state two ways to manufacture
ethanol in Question 3(d). They also struggled with the question on the separation of petroleum by
fractional distillation in Question 3(a)(ii).
• Questions on the topics of reactivity of metals, energy changes and electronic configuration were
answered reasonably well showing a good understanding of these topics.
notes.general_comments:
Many candidates tackled this paper well, showing a good knowledge of core chemistry. Good answers were
seen throughout the paper to several different questions. Most candidates found parts of every question
challenging. Nearly all candidates were entered at the appropriate level. It was evident that many candidates
are now using past paper practice as part of their revision programme, but more revision is needed on some
aspects of this syllabus.
Misinterpretation of the rubric happened in some cases. The most common misinterpretation was in
Question 2(d) which asked, ‘Describe the separation and motion of the particles in a solid’. Some
candidates got them mixed up and others got the terms separation and arrangement confused and wrote
down a correct answer for arrangement and not separation. Candidates also wrongly compared states. They
talked about ways of changing the state of the solid and so did not achieve any credit. Some candidates also
struggled with the question about how the rate of the reaction differed with a change in conditions. Many
candidates just talked incorrectly about increasing the amount of metal or volume of dilute sulfuric acid.
Some candidates struggled to name compounds from formulae and others did not know how to work out the
products from the electrolysis of a molten ionic compound. A few candidates thought that it was ‘bromide’
given off at one of the electrodes instead of ‘bromine’. The balancing of equations was done well,
demonstrating that candidates had practiced these as part of their revision. Candidates struggled with the
solubility rules and more work should be done to learn these rules in revision time closer to the examination.
Candidates struggled to give detailed answers to questions with the command words ‘deduce’ or ‘explain’.
They need to practice these types of questions when doing the past paper questions. Data handling type
questions could have been answered better. Candidates often made slight mistakes and were not precise
enough when answering these types of questions.
The standard of English was very good. Some candidates need to be more explicit when writing about
certain concepts and not use the words ‘it’ and ‘they’ to answer questions as these do not always make it
clear what is being referred to. Some better performing candidates wrote their answers as short phrases or
bullet points. Candidates are less likely to write vague statements or contradict themselves if this is done.
